items.title: Psychedelics Linked to Lower Anxiety and Depression in Young Adults
items.snippet: Do psychedelics benefit all ages equally? A study of over 1,000 adults from Durham University finds that classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD correlate with lower anxiety and depression in younger adults, but the mental health link fades entirely with advancing age.

items.title: Selfless Deed Paradox: Why Doing Good Matters More Than Pure Motives
items.snippet: Does a good deed count if it makes you feel good? Testing the famous "Friends" paradox, Ohio State researchers discovered that people don't judge helpers for mixed motives, finding "nice" and "kind" are functionally interchangeable while "caring" sets a higher bar.

items.snippet: Summary: A population-based epidemiological investigation from Trinity College Dublin finds no evidence connecting lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water with cognitive decline or dementia risk in older adults. items.title: How Fleeting Moments With Strangers Combat Loneliness
items.snippet: Can a warm smile from a stranger keep loneliness at bay? University of Georgia sociologist Joseph Hermanowicz coins the term "evanescent interactions" to explain how fleeting, empathetic micro-connections validate human existence and foster social belonging.

items.title: Low-Frequency Theta Waves Organize Frontal Cortex Cognition
items.snippet: How does the brain coordinate complex thought across distant regions? MIT researchers discovered that low-frequency theta waves act as the frontal cortex's master air traffic control, synchronizing neural spikes and orchestrating beta and gamma rhythms during flexible cognition.

items.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
items.snippet: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.

items.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
items.snippet: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

items.title: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you.
